extracted.intended_audience: plant breeders, growers, and inventors (and their counsel) considering U.S. intellectual property protection for novel plant varieties
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and obtaining plant-specific intellectual property in the U.S., comparing Plant Variety Protection Act (PVPA) certificates, U.S. plant patents, and utility patents, including statutory protections, filing deadlines, deposit and fee requirements, and scope of enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: PVPA eligibility after 2018 Farm Bill
rubrics_metrics.description: PVPA certificates are available for both asexually and sexually reproduced plant varieties following the 2018 Farm Bill amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formerly plant patents were for asexually reproduced varieties and the PVPA only for sexually reproducing varieties (seed‑produced). The 2018 change makes PVPA certificates available for both modes of reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term length comparison (plant patent vs PVPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A US plant patent term is 20 years from the filing date of the application; a PVPA certificate term runs from the date the certificate is granted and is 25 years for a tree or a vine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a plant patent term starts at filing, prosecution time shortens enforceable term (example: two years prosecution => 18 years enforceable). PVPA term runs from grant, which may provide a longer effective protection period for some asexually reproduced varieties (especially trees/vines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of protection: plant patent vs PVPA
rubrics_metrics.description: A US plant patent prevents asexual reproduction (cloning) of the particular variety identified in the patent; a PVPA certificate protects not only the particular variety but also certain varieties derived from the protected variety if they meet statutory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PVPA protection can therefore be broader than a plant patent because it can reach derived varieties, not just exact clones of the claimed variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringing acts under Section 2541(a) of Title 7 (complete list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute lists specific acts that constitute infringement of a protected variety under the PVPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists the full statutory acts: (1) sell/market/offer/expose for sale/deliver/ship/consign/exchange/solicit offer/any transfer of title or possession; (2) import into or export from the United States; (3) sexually or asexually multiply or propagate (including by tuber or part of a tuber) the variety as a step in marketing (for growing purposes); (4) use the variety in producing (as distinguished from developing) a hybrid or different variety therefrom; (5) use seed marked 'Unauthorized Propagation Prohibited' or 'Unauthorized Seed Multiplication Prohibited' or progeny thereof to propagate the variety; (6) dispense the variety to another, in a form which can be propagated, without notice that it is a protected variety; (7) condition the variety for the purpose of propagation, except to the extent conditioning is related to permitted activities under section 2543; (8) stock the variety for any of the purposes in paragraphs (1)–(7); (9) perform any of the foregoing acts even when the variety is multiplied other than sexually, except in pursuance of a valid United States plant patent; and (10) instigate or actively induce performance of any of the foregoing acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of infringement to related varieties under Section 2541(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain related varieties and materials are treated as infringing under PVPA unless exceptions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 2541(c) extends infringement to: (1) any variety that is essentially derived from a protected variety (unless the protected variety is an essentially derived variety); (2) any variety that is not clearly distinguishable from a protected variety; (3) any variety whose production requires the repeated use of a protected variety; and (4) harvested material (including entire plants and plant parts) obtained through unauthorized use of propagating material of a protected variety, unless the owner had a reasonable opportunity to exercise PVPA rights with respect to the propagating material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing deadlines and novelty/disclosure bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Both plant patents and PVPA applications must be filed within one (1) year of any sale or disposition of the variety in the United States; foreign sales have different bar periods depending on protection sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sale or disposition outside the U.S. more than one year prior will bar a US plant patent application. Under the PVPA, the foreign-sale period is extended: four years for a tuber-propagated plant, and six years for a tree or vine. Practitioners must track domestic and foreign commercialization dates to preserve rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: PVPA deposit and propagating material requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A PVPA application requires a deposit of plant material (propagating material); as of the page text the deposit requirement for asexually reproduced plants had been waived until January 6, 2023, but the applicant must submit a declaration about maintaining propagating material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deposit is required the applicant must provide plant material; when waived the applicant must still declare that propagating material will be maintained at a specific physical location subject to inspection and that the material will be provided to the Plant Variety Protection Office within 3 months of a request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and fee differences (PVPA vs plant patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: PVPA filing fees are significantly higher than plant patent filing fees: the page cites a PVPA filing fee of $5,150 versus $770 total for a US plant patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO patent filing fees may be reduced for small businesses and individuals; PVPA costs and deposit obligations can make it relatively more expensive. Cost should factor into choice of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility patent applicability for plants and plant-derived inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patents are available for aspects of plants such as plant cells, plant tissue cultures, plant parts, herbal medicines and supplements, chemicals made by plants, and novel plant varieties that result from human manipulation (e.g., genetic mutations or other interventions altering growth, yield, color, or other characteristics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility patents may cover molecular, cellular, biochemical, or process inventions related to plants, and may be preferable when the invention is not limited to a whole plant variety or when stronger/longer protection is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic recommendation: consider filing both PVPA and plant patent for asexually reproduced varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of differences in term length and scope, a grower should strongly consider filing both a US plant patent application and a PVPA application for new asexually reproduced plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dual filings can combine the benefits of both systems (e.g., plant patent protection and PVPA's reach to derived varieties or longer effective term for certain plants), but applicants should weigh costs, deposit requirements, and timing constraints.
